doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
title: Bob January's band and starting a rehearsal big band
summary: Led Bob January's stock band, then formed his own rehearsal band with Mel Lewis and others.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: to play if you loved swing music and loved big band music, the only way to play it in 1979 or ’80 for a young musician was in these kind of like second rate bands that played stock arrangements or transcriptions and you might have three or four really great players in the band and some others that weren’t so great. It was a lot of fun and it paid. But it was not at all excellent playing. So one of those bands was a band led by a guy named Bob January. And the singer in his band was Barbara Lea. And we became friends. And I was such a pain in the neck I guess at these rehearsals that Bob said, “Man, you know, you’re — why don’t you lead the band?” You know, that kind of thing, you know, screw you, that kind of thing. And I stood up you know and I’m going to lead the band and whatever. And I found out that — we were playing, I’ll never forget we were playing a stock arrangement of “920 Special.” And it turns out that there were four trumpets, the fourth trumpet player had a different stock arrangement. And they had been playing it for twenty years. And it was almost the same but a little bit different. And so I guess whoever played the fourth trumpet part would just modify it by listening. I said, “Can I see that part for a moment?” I thought this is the wrong arrangement. Well to jump, I decided to put together a big band. And I brought with me Robbie Scott was the drummer and Barbara Lea was singing and I must say I put together a band. I mean I started a rehearsal band. And I had some more music I had copied from Benny Goodman and then other people started to — I started to get some charts from different people — copies of this, I mean people like Bill Shremp and Dean Pratt and some other people who were also big band people and they had music. And we started to rehearse and it started to sound pretty good and as I mentioned I’d known, I forget how but I had met Mel Lewis. And I remember asking a friend, saying man I wonder if I could ask Mel to come down and rehearse. Well if you’re going to ask Mel, I mean for Christ’s sake, I mean he has his own band at the Vanguard. He said, “Well the worst he can do is say no.” So he came down, he made a rehearsal. I called some really good charts. And everybody in the band, I mean John Parisi was playing trumpet, Dick Sudhalter, a wonderful trombone player named Eph Resnick — E-P-H — you can look him up in the discographies. Bobby Pring, Bob Kindred, Akira Omori and I’m trying to think of who else you might know — some really really great players. Frank Tate played bass, and the drummer was Fred Stahl. Really great players. Well Mel came down and sat in, liked it and said I’ll come back next week. Well when Mel said he would come back next week, and no one’s getting paid, I mean I’m paying for the rehearsal space and taping all the music and copying all the charts, but I loved it. I had nothing else to do. When Mel started making it then all of a sudden well Danny Bank wants to play. Or, you know, or Eddie Bert, or Paulie Cohen or whomever. So I started to assemble a band that was a mixture of Doug Lawrence and Ken Peplowski and Chuck Wilson and Matt Finders and Tony Kadleck later, and young
